topic: HL Extension: Business Strategy and Decision Making
subject: business-studies

items.title: Share price and intrinsic value can diverge for years
items.claim: Robert Shiller's work (Nobel 2013) showed stock prices vary much more than fundamental dividends would justify. What's the implication for share price as a measure of company performance?

options.text: Share price always equals intrinsic value at all times
Share prices can diverge from intrinsic value for extended periods (excess volatility); managers focused on quarterly share prices may make worse long-term decisions
Share price has no link to fundamentals ever
Only private firms have intrinsic value

items.reveal_title: Markets price emotions as well as cash flows
items.reveal:
Shiller's 1981 American Economic Review paper showed S&P 500 prices fluctuated 5-13x more than dividend-based fair value would justify. Tech bubble peaks (2000, 2021) and crisis troughs (2009, 2020) bookend this excess volatility.

Warren Buffett quotes Benjamin Graham: 'In the short run the market is a voting machine, in the long run a weighing machine.' Managers paid largely in stock options can be incentivised to manage the voting machine rather than build long-term weight.
items.why: Headline share price moves often reflect investor sentiment as much as company performance. Compensation and strategy that anchor on share price import this volatility.

items.title: Ansoff said diversification was the riskiest growth strategy
items.claim: Igor Ansoff's 1957 'Strategies for Diversification' in Harvard Business Review introduced a 2x2 matrix. Which growth strategy did he flag as carrying highest risk?

options.text: Diversification (new product, new market) — combining product and market uncertainty multiplies risk

items.reveal:
Ansoff's matrix sequences risk: market penetration (existing product, existing market) is safest; product development and market development each add one source of uncertainty; diversification adds two.

Empirical work (Markides 1995, McKinsey 2010s) has supported this in aggregate: unrelated diversification destroys shareholder value more often than not. The 1960s conglomerate boom (ITT, Hanson) and its 1990s breakup vindicated Ansoff's warning.
items.why: Growth strategies look attractive on the upside; Ansoff's matrix forces you to articulate the downside risks for each route.

items.title: Break-even with multiple products needs a sales mix
items.claim: A bakery sells two products. Bread has £2 contribution per unit; cakes have £5. Fixed costs are £14,000. Without knowing the sales mix, what can you calculate?

options.text: You cannot calculate one break-even point — only break-even combinations or a break-even assuming a fixed sales mix ratio
Break-even is always the average contribution divided into fixed costs
You need the selling price as well

items.reveal:
If the bakery historically sells 3 loaves per cake, weighted contribution per 'bundle' = 3 x £2 + 1 x £5 = £11. Break-even = £14,000 / £11 = 1,273 bundles = 3,820 loaves + 1,273 cakes.

Change the mix and the break-even quantity changes. This is why textbook single-product break-even questions are misleading guides to multi-product reality. Real firms use 'weighted contribution' or 'break-even sales value' instead.
items.why: The simple Y = a + bX break-even chart assumes one product. Few real firms have only one product, which is why management accounting moves to contribution margin analysis.
